Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Maid
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Car Similarity: Similar cars, Media Exposure: Related media content, Positive Emotion Confusion: Positive emotions
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform, Smoking: I smoke
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Vignette:
Mateo was twenty-six and had already learned to keep his life small. Originally from a Latin American family and now living in the United States, he worked as a maid, moving quietly through other people’s homes and cleaning offices where he could stay busy and unremarkable. He was divorced, and the separation had unfolded alongside the months after the event he rarely described in full. What he did say, in careful fragments, was enough to make the shape of it clear: he had been detained and tortured by armed men, held under the authority of people in uniform who treated him as if he had no rights at all. He remembered the hard, controlled violence of it, the sense that any protest would only bring more pain, and the humiliation of being at the mercy of strangers who seemed to enjoy his fear. Even now, when he tried to tell it, he became more precise about details than feelings, as though exactness might keep him from being overwhelmed.

After he came to the United States, Mateo noticed that ordinary things could suddenly throw him back into that time. Cars were one of the worst. A similar sedan parked outside an apartment building, the shape of headlights in traffic, the sound of an engine slowing behind him on the street could make his body go taut before he had time to think. He would look up quickly, trying to identify the make and color, and if it resembled the vehicle connected to his detention, his chest would tighten and he would feel the urge to move away. Related media content also unsettled him. News footage, crime stories, even a passing clip of men in uniforms or a roadside stop on television could catch him off guard. He did not seek those things out, but they still found him in waiting rooms, in coworkers’ phones, or in the background at a client’s house, and he would become alert and distant for the rest of the day. What surprised him most was how positive emotion could also leave him uneasy. If he found himself laughing with a coworker or feeling a brief lift after finishing a good day’s work, he would sometimes catch himself and think, with a flash of confusion, that something bad must be about to happen. The feeling did not seem safe to trust, and joy could leave him unsettled rather than comforted.

Over time he built a life around not being reminded. If someone brought up prisons, police, military, or anything that sounded too close to what had happened, Mateo would change the subject or leave the room. He avoided being around authority figures or anyone in a uniform whenever he could. In his line of work, that sometimes meant taking longer routes to jobs to avoid courthouse buildings, security guards, or police on the street. It also meant turning down some cleaning work if it involved office towers with visible guards at the entrance, because he could feel himself becoming tense before he even crossed the threshold. These choices made his world narrower and, at times, more difficult to manage financially, but he told himself that keeping distance was safer than testing whether he could tolerate those reminders. He had also taken up smoking, especially during breaks and after upsetting encounters, holding the cigarette for a few minutes as something he could focus on when his mind became crowded.

At night, Mateo seldom slept straight through. He would wake in the dark, often without a dream he could remember, and immediately check whether he was safe. He listened for footsteps in the hallway, glanced at the door, and sometimes checked the window more than once before settling back down, only to wake again later and repeat the process. In the daytime he was hyperaware of strangers approaching him, even in ordinary settings like the sidewalk near the grocery store or the lobby of a building where he was cleaning. A person walking toward him too directly could make him brace, especially if they came from behind or seemed to close the distance quickly. He also reacted with alarm when someone touched him unexpectedly. A hand on his shoulder from a coworker, a client brushing past him in a narrow corridor, even a casual tap to get his attention could make him jolt and turn sharply before he recognized who it was.

By the time he sought help, Mateo was exhausted by the constant effort of staying on guard. He had begun to feel that his life was organized around preventing the next shock, yet he could not fully relax in his own apartment or at work. He came to therapy not because he thought talking would erase what had happened, but because he was tired of waking in the night to check the room, tired of flinching at touch, tired of scanning every approaching stranger as if danger might appear in the next second. What brought him in was the accumulation of these moments and the fear that they were now shaping everything he did. He hoped for relief, but more than that he hoped to feel safe enough to move through a day, or a night, without constantly preparing for harm.
